newsitem.title: CANADA: Queen Elizabeth marks Newfoundland anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Queen Elizabeth marks Newfoundland anniversary.

text.p: Queen Elizabeth joined thousands of Newfoundlanders on Tuesday to mark the 500th anniversary of explorer John Cabot's arrival at the site of this fishing port on North America's eastern edge.

Accompanied by her husband Prince Philip, Irish Prime Minister John Bruton and other dignitaries, the British queen was at quayside to meet "The Matthew" -- a 50-ton wooden replica of the vessel that Cabot sailed to the "new founde landes" in 1497.
The reproduction of Cabot's 75-foot (23-metre) caravel, was built in England and sailed from Bristol across the Atlantic to Bonavista harbor, where many historians believe Cabot landed.

"So Newfoundland became the link between the old and the new worlds," Queen Elizabeth said in a brief speech at the quayside, where the Cabot landfall was re-enacted. "It represents the geographical and intellectual beginning of modern North America.
The queen, who is Canada's head of state, arrived in Newfoundland on Monday for a 10-day tour of Canada, her 16th since becoming monarch in 1952.

Newfoundland, which has been hit hard by the collapse of its fishing industry after the depletion of what was once the richest cod fishing ground in the world, received C$20 million ($14.4 million) in government funding for a summer-long series of commemorations.
Newfoundlanders were in a party mood.

"This town really fell apart after the fishing stopped. A lot of people will go on welfare and some will lose their homes, but this (celebration) with the queen coming is bringing us together," said Angie Cuff, 17, who grew up in Bonavista.
The town of 4,600 people is on the east coast of Newfoundland, about 60 miles (96.56 km) north of the provincial capital, St. John's.

Crowds from across Newfoundland and Labrador braved cold, gray weather to throng the streets and dockside as "The Matthew" and its 19-man crew of Britons, Canadians and Australians sailed into Bonavista harbor.

After the discovery of the New World by Christopher Columbus five years earlier, the Italian-born Cabot, or Giovanni Caboto, was seeking a new trade route to the East Indies when he stumbled on Newfoundland and claimed it for England's King Henry VII, who bankrolled his odyssey.
Cabot's voyage, like much of his life, is shrouded in mystery. Cabot died in 1498, his ship's log was destroyed and few other first-hand historical records have been found.

Despite the celebrations in Newfoundland, where generations of schoolchildren have learned that Cabot first spotted land and exclaimed, "O buono vista" ("Oh happy sight"), there is a debate over whether Cabot ever saw the place, let alone landed here.
Some scholars say strong Labrador currents carried him down the coast so he missed Newfoundland entirely and landed instead near Cape Breton in Nova Scotia.

Ironically, this theory was embraced by many Canadian historians before Newfoundland joined Canada in 1949. After Newfoundland became Canada's 10th province, Canadian scholars became increasingly convinced that Cabot's landfall had in fact been in Newfoundland.
Residents of Cape Breton are having none of it. They are sticking to their claim to fame and plan their own celebrations of Cabot's landings in Cape Breton -- four days from now.
